evidence.claim: Section 158 says the King appoints the Prime Minister on House approval, the Council of Ministers acts by collective responsibility, and the Prime Minister cannot hold office for more than eight years in total.
evidence.title: Constitution of the Kingdom of Thailand B.E. 2560 (2017)
evidence.publisher: Office of the Council of State via CYRILLA
evidence.excerpt: Section 158 says the King appoints the Prime Minister on House approval, the Council of Ministers acts by collective responsibility, and the Prime Minister cannot hold office for more than eight years in total.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary constitutional text from an official legal translation repository.
evidence.period_fit: Sets the constitutional authority and hard constraint in force during 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Defines the institutional limits of Prayut's office rather than a personal nuclear mandate.
contrary_evidence: This is general executive authority, not nuclear-specific authority.

evidence.claim: The House voted 256 confidence, 206 no-confidence, and 9 abstentions for Gen. Prayut Chan-o-cha, identified there as Prime Minister and Minister of Defense.
evidence.title: The 14th session of the 25th House of Representatives meeting, 4th year (First Annual Ordinary Session), a special meeting
evidence.publisher: Secretariat of the House of Representatives
evidence.excerpt: The House voted 256 confidence, 206 no-confidence, and 9 abstentions for Gen. Prayut Chan-o-cha, identified there as Prime Minister and Minister of Defense.
evidence.source_locator: vote result paragraph in the article summary
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official parliamentary vote record with exact counts.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributes the vote to Prayut's office-holding government.
contrary_evidence: Parliamentary support is not evidence of responsible existential-risk conduct.

evidence.claim: Thai PBS reported the court's 6 to 3 ruling that Prayut's prime-ministerial clock counted from 2017 and that he had not yet reached the eight-year limit.
evidence.title: มติศาลรัฐธรรมนูญเสียงข้างมาก ชี้ "ประยุทธ์" เป็นนายกฯยังไม่ครบ 8 ปี
evidence.excerpt: Thai PBS reported the court's 6 to 3 ruling that Prayut's prime-ministerial clock counted from 2017 and that he had not yet reached the eight-year limit.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent local-language reporting on the final ruling the same day.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Reports the court's ruling on Prayut's tenure and return to office.
contrary_evidence: The ruling is a legal tenure decision, not evidence of existential-risk management.

evidence.claim: Thailand has a safeguards agreement in force under the NPT and an additional protocol in force with the IAEA.
evidence.title: Country List : Office of Legal Affairs : IAEA
evidence.excerpt: Thailand has a safeguards agreement in force under the NPT and an additional protocol in force with the IAEA.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Authoritative IAEA treaty/status record for Thailand.
evidence.period_fit: State-level safeguards posture was in force during 2022 and is relevant background.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Institutional state commitment, not a personal Prayut choice.
contrary_evidence: This confirms safeguards infrastructure, but not who personally drove it in 2022.

evidence.claim: The Nuclear Energy for Peace Act 2016, as amended, is the governing law listed for Thailand's nuclear activities and related regulation.
evidence.title: กฎหมาย
evidence.publisher: Office of Atoms for Peace, Thailand
evidence.excerpt: The Nuclear Energy for Peace Act 2016, as amended, is the governing law listed for Thailand's nuclear activities and related regulation.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary regulatory-law listing from the agency responsible for nuclear safety.
evidence.period_fit: This is the legal framework governing Thai civil nuclear oversight in 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Institutional framework, not direct Prayut command-and-control evidence.
contrary_evidence: A regulatory statute exists regardless of whether the ruler personally intervened in it.

evidence.claim: Thailand signed the CTBT in 1996 and ratified it in 2018; the page explains that the treaty bans nuclear testing and that Thailand operates IMS and national data-center functions for verification.
evidence.title: สนธิสัญญาว่าด้วยการห้ามทดลองนิวเคลียร์โดยสมบูรณ์ (Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty: CTBT)
evidence.publisher: Office of Atoms for Peace, Thailand
evidence.excerpt: Thailand signed the CTBT in 1996 and ratified it in 2018; the page explains that the treaty bans nuclear testing and that Thailand operates IMS and national data-center functions for verification.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Primary Thai CTBT implementation page with treaty dates and monitoring infrastructure.
evidence.period_fit: Strong background on Thailand's anti-test posture and verification role in 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: State treaty posture, not a Prayut-specific nuclear decision.
contrary_evidence: CTBT ratification long predates 2022 and is not proof of any new action by Prayut.

evidence.claim: Thailand states that it supports arms control and disarmament and has a firm policy not to develop, acquire, or proliferate any kind of WMD or their delivery systems.
evidence.title: Thailand and Disarmament
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand
evidence.excerpt: Thailand states that it supports arms control and disarmament and has a firm policy not to develop, acquire, or proliferate any kind of WMD or their delivery systems.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official MFA policy statement page, updated during the 2022 period.
evidence.ruler_attribution: State policy, not a Prayut-only initiative.
contrary_evidence: This is a standing policy page and does not show a specific 2022 ruler choice.

evidence.claim: Thailand attended the first TPNW States Parties meeting, said the treaty complements existing disarmament and non-proliferation mechanisms, and is one of the first three countries to have signed and ratified on the first day it opened.
evidence.title: Permanent Secretary for Foreign Affairs reaffirmed Thailand’s commitment towards the achievement of a World Free of Nuclear Weapons at the First Meeting of States Parties to the TPNW
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand
evidence.excerpt: Thailand attended the first TPNW States Parties meeting, said the treaty complements existing disarmament and non-proliferation mechanisms, and is one of the first three countries to have signed and ratified on the first day it opened.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct contemporaneous MFA reporting on Thailand's 2022 treaty diplomacy.
evidence.period_fit: Directly within 2022 and relevant to treaty/diplomatic posture.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Handled by the foreign-affairs apparatus under Prayut's government, not by a nuclear command role.
contrary_evidence: The delegation was institutional, not proof of Prayut's personal involvement in each talking point.

evidence.claim: Thailand's 2022 ARF nonproliferation priorities included the NPT's three pillars, full implementation of the Bangkok Treaty, complementarity between the TPNW and the NPT, peaceful nuclear uses with safety, security, and safeguards, and confidence-building around emerging technologies.
evidence.title: Thailand hosted the 13th ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF) Inter-Sessional Meeting on Non-Proliferation and Disarmament (ISM on NPD)
evidence.publisher: Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Kingdom of Thailand
evidence.excerpt: Thailand's 2022 ARF nonproliferation priorities included the NPT's three pillars, full implementation of the Bangkok Treaty, complementarity between the TPNW and the NPT, peaceful nuclear uses with safety, security, and safeguards, and confidence-building around emerging technologies.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous MFA report on Thailand-hosted regional nonproliferation diplomacy.
evidence.period_fit: Directly relevant to 2022 and to dual-use / safeguards governance.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Institutional foreign-policy posture, not a personal nuclear choice by Prayut.
contrary_evidence: The speaker was a senior official, so this does not show personal hands-on risk governance by the PM.

evidence.claim: Thailand's action record shows ratification of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons on 2021-01-22.
evidence.title: Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons
evidence.excerpt: Thailand's action record shows ratification of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons on 2021-01-22.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Authoritative UN depositary record for treaty ratification.
evidence.period_fit: Important inherited treaty posture that carried into 2022.
evidence.ruler_attribution: State ratification, not a 2022 personal executive act by Prayut.
contrary_evidence: Ratification predates 2022, so it is inherited baseline rather than a fresh 2022 decision.

evidence.claim: UNODA reported that Thailand hosted the ASEAN UNSCR 1540 workshop in Bangkok and reaffirmed its solid commitment to implementing the resolution against WMD proliferation to non-state actors.
evidence.title: ASEAN States meet to strengthen implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 1540
evidence.publisher: United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs
evidence.excerpt: UNODA reported that Thailand hosted the ASEAN UNSCR 1540 workshop in Bangkok and reaffirmed its solid commitment to implementing the resolution against WMD proliferation to non-state actors.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct UNODA report, contemporaneous with the 2022 workshop, though the open page was not fetched in full.
evidence.period_fit: Directly in 2022 and relevant to WMD/dual-use controls.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Government of Thailand commitment, not personal Prayut authorship.
contrary_evidence: The event reflects institutional commitment, not proof of Prayut's personal oversight of dual-use controls.

unresolved_gaps: No Prayut-specific 2022 nuclear or other existential-risk choice is evidenced; the package is mostly inherited treaty and safeguards context.
No direct cabinet-minute or NSC record ties Prayut personally to each 2022 Ukraine or Myanmar diplomatic position.
Direct command-chain evidence for specific police operations, protest policing, and protest-prosecution decisions is limited.
Direct documentary proof of Prayut's personal authorization of spyware or surveillance is absent.
Ruler-level evidence on appointments quality and 2022 rule-setting for competition, property rights, and investment remains thin.
Outcome evidence is stronger than direct ruler attribution across health, education, and social protection.
No direct 2022 evidence of hidden assets, family profit, or proven deception beyond disclosure opacity and allegations.
There is no single consolidated FY2022 execution audit tying the program, implementation, and outcomes back to Prayut's full cabinet-level agenda.
